title: Settings in a booking product
metaTitle: Booking settings are a small cabinet
excerpt: Booking settings are a cabinet, not a second product a hurried guest must learn. Group reminders, timezone, and who the booking is for. Bury the rest.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, a calm field with no second task hiding in it.
caption: The cabinet should be this quiet: a few bands, easy to tell apart. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which booking settings does a guest actually change?
faqs.answer: They change timezone, how you remind them, and sometimes who the booking is for. Those belong at the top of the cabinet and, when they affect this booking, on the booking itself. Payment methods and invoices matter at the moment of payment. Marketing opt-in and connected apps are rare, and they should not lead the screen.

faqs.question: Should timezone live only in settings?
faqs.answer: The default can live in settings. The time they are about to book has to show the zone on that screen, with a way to change it without a scavenger hunt. A guest on a phone, in a hurry, will not open a cabinet to discover they are about to book the wrong hour. Show the zone beside the time.

faqs.question: What should be hard to find?
faqs.answer: Delete account, staff scheduling rules, API keys, and tax setup should be hard for a guest to stumble into. Findable for the person who needs them, buried for everyone else. A guest cabinet that looks like an admin console teaches them that changing a reminder is a technical task. It is not.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Booking product settings UX is a cabinet, not a second product. A guest on a phone, in a hurry, changes a few things: the timezone, the reminder, and who the booking is for. Group those. Bury the rest. They came to leave with a time, not to learn a preferences system.

If the only way to avoid a wrong-hour booking is a settings page they never open, the settings page has been given a job that belongs on the calendar. The cabinet holds defaults. The booking screen holds the decision for this visit.

## What a guest changes often

Reminders are the frequent change. Email, text, or both. How far ahead. A single "Remind me" with one clear default is better than a matrix they must complete before the booking counts. After they have a booking, the confirmation can offer the same control again. People understand reminders when they can see the time they might forget.

Timezone is the other frequent change, and it is urgent. Detect the phone zone. Print it in words next to every time you show. Let them change it on that screen. Saving the choice into settings is good. Forcing a trip into settings to discover the zone is how you get a guest who arrives an hour early and angry.

Who the booking is for matters when someone books a child, a client, or a colleague. If your product allows that, the form field is the setting for this booking, and the cabinet can remember the last answer. If your product does not allow it, do not put a decorative "Participants" page in settings that errors on save.

Accessibility of the appointment itself sometimes belongs here too, if the guest must say they need step-free access or a longer slot. Put that on the service or the booking, in the flow, if it changes what you can offer. A buried checkbox they find after they arrive is too late. The cabinet is the wrong room for a fact you needed at booking time.

Nielsen Norman Group's research, summarized by Jakob Nielsen, says people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds and read only a fraction of a page. A settings index full of equal icons fails that test. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a reason to lead with Reminders and Timezone, in words, and to leave the rest further in.

## What to bury

Payment methods belong near payment, and a saved-card list can live in Account for the person who returns. They should not be the first row a guest sees when they only wanted to silence a text. Lead with the thing they came to change.

Invoices and tax details are rare and real. Put them under Account or Receipts. A guest looking for a receipt should find a list of their bookings with a receipt on each, not a general ledger. The booking is the object they remember. Attach the paper to the object.

Marketing email is a single choice, written as a sentence, defaulted off unless they opted in at booking. Do not bury a pre-ticked box in settings and call it preference management. Do not put a newsletter template picker on a guest cabinet.

Connected calendars are optional and a little dangerous. "Add to my calendar" on the confirmation does the job for most guests. A standing connection that can read their week is a bigger ask. If you offer it, explain what you read and what you write, in the group where the connection lives, not in a terms PDF only.

Staff tools, service durations, buffers, and cancellation policy editors are not guest settings. They are the business cabinet. A guest who can see "Buffer minutes" will tap it, meet a denial, and decide your app is broken. Hide staff tools from the guest session entirely.

Delete account sits at the end of Account, with a sentence about upcoming bookings. Say whether a future time is cancelled or kept. That consequence is the design. A red button alone is not a design.

## Do not make them finish settings to finish a booking

The booking flow should assume defaults. Phone timezone. A reminder by email to the address they just typed. The attendee is the person named on the form. They can change any of those without visiting a cabinet first.

A setup wizard that demands notification permission, a photo, and a password before showing times is a tour with required fields. Skip it. Create what you need after they have a time, and only what you need. A password can wait until they ask to manage the booking later.

When a setting changes the meaning of the screen they are on, reflect it immediately. Changing timezone updates the times in place. Changing reminder updates the sentence on the confirmation: "We will email you the morning of the booking." If they have to imagine the effect, the control is too far from the object.

Write the cabinet and the booking in the same nouns. If settings say "SMS alerts" and the confirmation says "text reminder," pick one. Text is the word guests use. Use it in both places.

## Shape the cabinet for one thumb

Four groups are plenty. Reminders. Timezone, if it is not only on the booking. Payment. Account. Profile is optional and usually vanity on a booking product. Do not add Profile because other apps have it.

On a phone, the index is those words. One group opens one short screen. A single page of every switch forces precision scrolling and mistaken taps. Hurried guests mis-tap. Short screens forgive that.

Return them to the booking they came from. Settings opened from a confirmation should close to that confirmation, not to a marketing homepage. The landmark is the time they hold. Keep it in the header while they change a reminder, so they remember which booking they are editing.

Switches save immediately and say so. Text fields, such as the name on the booking, need an explicit save if leaving the field might lose a half-edited name. Tell them when it is saved. A silent failure here means they arrive and you have the wrong name.

Respect reduced motion and text size from the operating system. A guest who enlarged text should still see the reminder sentence without horizontal clipping. If the cabinet only works at the default size, it does not work on the phone they are actually holding.

## Staff settings are a different cabinet

The owner changes hours, services, and who can be booked. That product can be dense. It is not this article's screen, and it must not share a navigation with the guest. Separate hosts. Separate home screens. The guest home is their next booking. The owner home is today's schedule.

If you are tempted to reuse one settings shell for both, you will leak a staff row into the guest list the first time someone adds a toggle in a hurry. Split them. The guest cabinet can stay small enough to read in a minute. That limit is a feature.

Language is a reasonable guest setting if you serve more than one. Put it in Account. Do not auto-switch the confirmation away from the language they booked in because their phone is set differently, without showing the control. Say which language the reminder will use.


A guest who books for someone else should not inherit a cabinet full of that person's payment history. If you store a card, show it only after they authenticate as the account holder, and say whose card it is. A shared family phone that opens settings and lists a card nickname is a privacy failure, not a convenience. Prefer the confirmation as the receipt, and keep the account page quiet until they ask.

The language of the reminder is part of the reminder setting, not a buried locale code. A sentence such as text me in English is something a guest can judge. A locale tag is a developer setting that slipped into the cabinet. If you only send one language, omit the control. A control that does not change the text is a promise they will test once and then distrust, including the switches that do work.
## Review the cabinet, then walk onto the floor

On a phone, as a guest with one upcoming time, open settings. Reminders should be first. Change the reminder. Return. The confirmation should state the new reminder without a reload mystery. Change timezone and confirm the time you already booked was converted visibly, not silently shifted.

Open the same account's settings and look for staff words. If you see buffers, webhooks, or another guest's details, the cabinet is the wrong product.

The next first screen in this set is not a guest at all. It is the person standing on a warehouse floor with an item in their hand. That piece is [the first screen of an inventory tool](/blog/the-first-screen-of-an-inventory-tool). Do not reuse this cabinet there. The frequent change on the floor is the zone they are standing in, not a reminder about Tuesday.

If a booking flow and its cabinet should be designed together, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The guest should finish the errand and get back to the time. Anything that feels like a second product is in the way.
